hints: Look carefully at the number of rings in each base outline. Which one, nucleotide 1 or nucleotide 2, has two fused rings and which has only one ring?

Remember the two pairing rules in DNA: a double-ring purine always pairs with a single-ring pyrimidine, and the number of dashed hydrogen bonds tells you if it is an A-T pair (2 bonds) or a G-C pair (3 bonds).
walkthrough:
**Spot purine versus pyrimidine from ring number**

Great start, just count the rings. Nucleotide 1 has two fused rings, a 5-sided plus a 6-sided ring, so it is a purine. Nucleotide 2 has only one 6-sided ring, so it is a pyrimidine.

Rule to remember: purines (adenine and guanine) = double ring, pyrimidines (thymine and cytosine) = single ring.

**Use the hydrogen bonds to name the pair**

Now look at the dashed lines. There are exactly two hydrogen bonds holding this pair together.

In DNA: $$A-T \text{ pair} = 2 \text{ hydrogen bonds}$$ $$G-C \text{ pair} = 3 \text{ hydrogen bonds}$$
So two bonds must mean an adenine-thymine pair.

**Put the two clues together**

Nucleotide 1 is the double-ring purine in an A-T pair, so it must be adenine. Nucleotide 2 is the single-ring pyrimidine in an A-T pair, so it must be thymine. That matches row A perfectly.

options.A: Correct and well done. Nucleotide 1 is double-ringed so is the purine adenine, nucleotide 2 is single-ringed so is the pyrimidine thymine, and 2 hydrogen bonds confirms an A-T pair.
options.B: Not quite. Cytosine is a single-ring pyrimidine but nucleotide 1 is double-ringed, and a C-G pair would need 3 hydrogen bonds, not 2.
options.C: Not quite. Guanine is double-ringed like nucleotide 1, but a G-C pair needs 3 hydrogen bonds, not the 2 shown here.
options.D: Close on the pair but swapped. Thymine is a single-ring pyrimidine so it cannot be nucleotide 1 which is double-ringed, and adenine cannot be the single-ring nucleotide 2.
